extracted.intended_audience: NIH extramural investigators, grant applicants, peer reviewers, and biomedical research policy-interested readers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critique about how NIH grant applications (new and competing continuations/renewals) are evaluated, how peer review behaviors (scores, study section discussion, reviewer load) affect outcomes, and how NIH policy choices (modular cap, programmatic pickups, affirmative action) interact with applicant behavior and equity. Primarily aimed at understanding review criteria and system-level incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Productivity (papers resulting from prior award)
rubrics_metrics.description: Were you productive? Did the prior interval of support produce publications?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers value both quantity and quality of publications produced under the prior award. 'Glamour' (high-profile) papers can strongly sway panels; ordinary but solid productivity also helps. Berg’s data (avg ~6 papers per $250K full modular award; IQR ~4-11) are cited to set expectations. Productivity is judged relative to field norms and can be treated as minimum expected output (bare minimum vs outstanding). Multi-award PIs attributing multiple grants to papers can complicate crediting. The renewal is submitted with the final year still to go, so publications up to that point are considered. Explanations and context (e.g., slow-to-publish study types) matter to reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressing original Specific Aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Did the project complete or adequately address the Specific Aims proposed in the prior award?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some reviewers place heavy weight on whether each proposed Aim was executed; others accept reasonable deviations. A competing continuation that has clearly addressed original Aims (with published data or preliminary data ready-to-submit) is often viewed positively. However, grants are not contracts—scientific pivots, being scooped, or justified changes in direction can be acceptable if explained. Reviewers may penalize failure to address Aims, especially if no rationale or productivity exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment with overarching project goals / thematic productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if specific Aims changed, has the prior work contributed to the broad theme or overall goals of the project?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers consider whether publications and progress align with the overarching programmatic goals described in the original application. Applicants should explicitly state how productivity maps to the big-picture goals in the Progress Report. If productivity is moderate, alignment with the mission of the prior award can ameliorate concerns about not hitting every Aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progress Report completeness (list of publications and accomplishments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the renewal include a thorough Progress Report detailing what was accomplished and listing publications resulting from the prior award?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competitive continuations are expected to include a Progress Report and publication list; reviewers use these to judge past performance. The Progress Report is the vehicle to show alignment with prior aims, productivity, and to explain deviations or failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence / Preliminary Data for renewal
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the renewal include appropriate preliminary data demonstrating progress toward future aims?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For renewals, reviewers expect preliminary data or publications that support the feasibility of the proposed continuation. If prior work generated publishable data that supports next aims, that strengthens the application. Lack of supporting preliminary data can be a weakness, especially if prior productivity was limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigator criterion / biosketch past performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the PI and team qualified and have they shown past productivity/capacity (as evidenced in the biosketch and prior funding)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'Investigator' criterion (one of the NIH's five major criteria) is used to assess the PI's track record and capability. The biosketch (listing papers and prior grants) inevitably prompts reviewers to judge program-level competence; prior successful use of funding influences confidence in future work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prior score/percentile and summary statement in renewal review
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the prior summary statement, score, or percentile influence reviewers of the competing continuation?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers see the prior summary statement and score; this can bias discussion. Some reviewers may react negatively if they feel prior funding was undeserved or think an application was a Programmatic pickup. The prior score may color perception of the renewal's merit even though the renewal should be judged on both past productivity and future plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative assessment and score spreading (reviewer calibration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do reviewers calibrate and spread scores relative to the set of applications they review, and how does that affect scoring?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIH review is comparative; reviewers tend to 'spread' scores across their pile. Reviewer load (number of applications assigned) affects how compressed or spread out scores are. SROs exhort score spreading to avoid clustering. The dynamics of score calibration influence whether small differences map onto fundable/unfundable outcomes; percentile attempts to adjust for inter-panel differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of reviewer load on scoring behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: How many applications a reviewer is assigned affects the distribution and calibration of their scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower reviewer loads (e.g., 5–6 applications) tend to produce less compressed scoring and may allow better discrimination; very low loads (3 apps) or atypical loads can distort typical scoring behavior. Experimental studies that simulate review must mimic real reviewer loads to be valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of study section discussion in score variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Does convened panel discussion (study section) reduce variability and produce different scoring outcomes compared with silent or simulated review?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study section discussion promotes score calibration and convergence among reviewers; omitting real discussion (or simulating it without actually convening) increases variability and can bias experiments toward null findings. Valid replication or experimental studies should include authentic panel discussion elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range restriction and selection of proposals in peer-review studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Does using only funded (or only discussed) proposals in an experiment introduce restriction-of-range bias when evaluating reviewer behavior?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting only funded or revised-into-funded proposals excludes low-quality/unscored grants and narrows the quality range, which can mask bias or reduce generalizability. Studies should include a representative range (including ND/low-quality applications) to reflect real NIH review dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation of experimental review scores with original scores (external validity control)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do scores from an experimental re-review correlate with the original real-world scores, and is that correlation consistent across manipulations (e.g., PI name changes)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparing experimental scores to original scores provides an important control to show whether the experiment replicates the actual quality ordering of applications. Lack of correlation suggests the experimental setup failed to capture real review determinants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Programmatic pickups / exception funding behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Does Programmatic funding (picking up grants out of order) influence fairness and review incentives?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programmatic pickups (awarding grants outside normal paylines) are common and can be applied for many reasons; they both stabilize favored investigators and introduce perceived inequities. NIH’s ad hoc pickups affect career stability and can be used (but are not consistently used) to address disparities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability of funding versus project-based funding tradeoff
rubrics_metrics.description: Should NIH pursue funder policies that prioritize stability (program-based support) versus strictly project-based selection?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stability helps labs maintain continuity and reduces churn; program-based emphasis (past performance, renewals) resembles HHMI-style funding and benefits established investigators. Conversely, too much program-based funding can reduce turnover and opportunities for newcomers. Policy choices must balance stability, diversity, and innovation; reviewers and NIH leadership often mix program- and project-based assessment implicitly in review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modular cap / requested direct costs behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: How do the modular budget cap ($250K direct historically) and inflation affect applicant budgeting behavior and review outcomes?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the modular cap captured most applications historically, applicants clustered at cap amounts; erosion of purchasing power with inflation causes more requests over the cap and more applications simply asking the maximum. Policy changes to cap levels affect submission behavior and may change aggregate success rates; NIH should model these effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity interventions (affirmative action / quota pickups) as a corrective metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Can programmatic pickups or quotas be used by NIH to redress observed demographic disparities in success rates?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The blog argues that relatively small numbers of strategic pickups (e.g., a few grants per IC per year/decade) could eliminate observed racial or other disparities, because the absolute numbers required are small. It criticizes NIH for not using routine pickup behavior to correct inequities in practice despite routinely picking up grants for other programmatic reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: K99/R00 success and conversion rates as equity/performance metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use success rates and R00 conversion percentages by race/ethnicity as a measure of differential outcomes in career-transition awards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported K99 success and R00 conversion disparities (e.g., Black applicants with lower success and lower conversion) provide concrete metrics to evaluate bias. Small absolute numbers (e.g., tens of grants) could be targeted to fix disparities; the blog highlights this as an actionable metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of funded vs unfunded proposals in studying peer review realism
rubrics_metrics.description: Does choosing only funded/revised grants in experiments misrepresent the true variability and behavior of peer reviewers?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including only grants that were funded (often after revision) biases the sample to those that could be salvaged by revision and may not represent the broad set of applications reviewers encounter. Experiments should mirror the proportion of ND (not discussed) applications and the true distribution of grant quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publications-per-dollar as an efficiency metric (punctuated use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Are publications per grant dollar (papers per $100k or per $250K) a legitimate 'efficiency' metric to evaluate grant productivity?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIH sometimes invokes metrics like pubs per direct cost to claim efficiency. The blog references Berg and others noting averages and wide IQR; warns against over-interpreting such metrics because multi-award PIs, field differences, and publication types complicate attribution and fairness.
